articles.title: Roman lifts off on a mission to survey the infrared sky
articles.description:
Image:
			
NASA’s Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope lifted off on a SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket from NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida, USA, at 07:26 EDT / 12:26 BST/ 13:26 CEST on 30 August 2026. With the successful launch, Roman began its mission to survey the sky in visible to near-infrared light to help reveal the nature of dark energy and dark matter. The telescope will also investigate the true diversity of exoplanets in our galaxy.
Roman is a NASA-led mission to which the European Space Agency (ESA) contributed star trackers, batteries, and detectors for the coronagraph instrument. ESA will also provide communications support through its deep-space ground station network, and enable data download using its new 35-metre antenna in New Norcia, Australia.
“I warmly congratulate our colleagues at NASA on the successful launch of Roman,” says Carole Mundell, ESA’s Director of Science. “ESA is proud to have provided essential hardware and to continue supporting Roman’s ambitious scientific goals. Together, we are opening new windows on the cosmos.”
Like ESA’s Euclid space telescope, Roman will enable astronomers to study the Universe in unprecedented detail. It is equipped with a primary mirror of 2.4 m and two instruments: the Wide Field Instrument (WFI) and a Coronagraph Instrument technology demonstration.
With its panoramic view of the sky, crisp infrared vision and quick re-orientation skills, Roman will perform fast and efficient surveys of a large area of the sky. By doing so, it will map clustering of galaxies over time and space and also study the light coming from thousands of distant type Ia supernovas which will help astronomers trace the expansion of the Universe.
“Roman should provide our clearest picture yet of whether dark energy is truly constant or whether it evolves over cosmic time – either outcome would have profound implications for our understanding of the Universe. I'm also excited by Roman's exoplanet census, which will discover thousands of new worlds, including cold planets and free-floating planets that have remained largely beyond our reach until now,” says Bethan James, ESA’s Roman Project Scientist. “Perhaps what excites me most is the unexpected. With its unprecedented combination of depth, area, and image quality, Roman has every opportunity to surprise us.”
After launch, Roman is on a steady course to the second Sun-Earth Lagrange point (L2), nearly 1.5 million km away from Earth. This location allows the telescope to have an unobstructed view of a wide area of the sky, almost 12%. Like ESA’s Euclid and the NASA/ESA/CSA James Webb Space Telescope, Roman will move in a wider orbit around the L2 point – much larger than the Moon’s orbit around Earth.
In the next three months following launch, the Roman team will conduct a carefully orchestrated series of deployments, calibrations, and tests. Once the commissioning period is complete, the mission will begin its science operations, starting with the first science image release. Roman will spend at least five years scanning the infrared sky and is designed to work in space for another five years.
[Image description: A SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket with NASA’s Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope on board is seen transiting the Sun during launch from Launch Complex 39A, on Sunday 30 August 2026, at NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida, US.]
articles.summary: NASA's Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope launches aboard a SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket, beginning its mission to map the infrared universe.

articles.title: Watch live: BepiColombo begins its arrival at Mercury
articles.description:
After eight years, the ESA/JAXA BepiColombo mission is about to enter its Mercury Arrival Phase. On 3 September 2026, ESA’s Mercury Transfer Module (MTM) will separate from BepiColombo’s two science orbiters – the first major step in one of the most operationally challenging planetary arrival sequences ever attempted by ESA.  
The European Space Agency (ESA) will livestream the critical milestone from 13:45 CEST. Tune in and witness the first step of one of the most complex phases of the mission, live from ESA mission control.  
Join ESA's livestream on YouTube here!
articles.summary: The ESA/JAXA BepiColombo mission is entering its Mercury arrival phase after eight years of travel, marking a landmark moment in planetary exploration.

articles.title: A New Catalog of Close to 3,000 Supernova Challenges Theories on Dark Energy
articles.description: The most comprehensive catalogue of exploding white dwarf stars ever assembled has revealed new clues about dark energy, the mysterious force driving the universe’s accelerating expansion.
articles.summary: A comprehensive catalog of nearly 3,000 supernovae from exploding white dwarfs provides new insights into dark energy and the universe's expansion.

articles.title: NASA's next great observatory could spot oceans on distant worlds
articles.description: We've found more than 5,500 exoplanets so far. Dozens of them are in the habitable zones of their parent stars, where, at least in theory, they could host an ocean. But we've never definitively found a liquid ocean on another planet.
articles.source: Space News - Space, Astronomy, Space Exploration
articles.summary: NASA's next-generation observatory will have the capability to detect oceans on distant exoplanets, potentially identifying habitable worlds.

articles.title: Researchers pinpoint key early-universe measurement with record precision
articles.description: An international team, including researchers from the University of Minnesota Twin Cities, has reached a major milestone in "precision cosmology" by measuring the amount of helium created in the universe's first five minutes with unprecedented accuracy.
articles.source: Space News - Space, Astronomy, Space Exploration
articles.summary: An international research team achieves record-breaking precision in measuring early universe parameters, advancing our understanding of cosmic origins.

articles.title: On this day in space! NASA astronaut Mae Jemison makes history as the 1st Black woman in space
articles.description: On Sept. 12, 1992, NASA astronaut Mae Jemison became the first African American woman to go to space. Here's why it mattered.
articles.summary: On September 12, 1992, NASA astronaut Mae Jemison made history as the first African American woman to reach space, marking a milestone in human spaceflight. This historic achievement continues to inspire future generations of space explorers.

articles.description:
A glimpse of a celestial wanderer that last visited during the Middle Ages—caught not by professional observatories, but by four amateurs with a telescope and patience.
The post Four amateur astronomers using a telescope in Chile’s Atacama desert found a come…
articles.summary: Amateur astronomers discover a rare comet in Chile's Atacama Desert 81 days before its closest approach, marking its first observed return in 1,900 years.

articles.title: Is it a planet or a moon? Scientists discover a strange Jupiter-sized world orbiting a brown dwarf in a never-before-seen cosmic system
articles.description: Astronomers found a massive object orbiting a brown dwarf star. This discovery challenges existing definitions of planets and moons. The unusual system features a nested orbital arrangement unlike our solar system. Scientists are debating the object's classif…
articles.summary: Astronomers discover a Jupiter-sized object orbiting a brown dwarf in an unprecedented configuration, challenging conventional definitions of planets and moons.

articles.title: On 5 September 1977 Voyager 1 left Cape Canaveral at 721.9 kg; as of 21 August 2024 it was 164.7 AU from Earth, moving about 38,027 mph relative to the Sun and still returning data
articles.description:
Nearly five decades after launch, humanity's most distant emissary continues whispering back from the edge of the solar system, defying every expectation of how long a machine can survive in the void.
The post On 5 September 1977 Voyager 1 left Cape Canaveral…
articles.summary: Voyager 1, launched in 1977, continues transmitting data from 164.7 AU away, demonstrating humanity's greatest achievement in deep space exploration after nearly five decades.

articles.description: Two galaxies merge at a furious rate in this Aug. 25, 2026, image of the II Zw 096 system. This and several other images of both visually and scientifically interesting galaxies were released by NASA’s Chandra X-ray Observatory and other telescopes. Chandra X-ray data (magenta) pinpoint powerful black hole activity and hot gas, while optical […]
articles.summary: NASA's Chandra X-ray Observatory captures a spectacular image of two galaxies merging in the II Zw 096 system, revealing the violent dynamics of galactic collisions.

articles.title: NASA Boosts Open Science, Data Sharing with Artemis Accords
articles.description: The science from every Moon rock sample, lunar dataset, and discovery produced through NASA’s Artemis program will be shared by the agency with the global scientific community. That commitment is upheld by all 71 countries that have signed the Artemis Accords, a set of principles for safe and transparent civil space exploration. NASA put those […]
articles.summary: NASA commits to open science principles through the Artemis Accords, ensuring that all lunar discoveries and data are shared with the global scientific community.

articles.title: BepiColombo begins Mercury arrival with MTM separation success
articles.description: On 3 September 2026 at 15:49 CEST, the European Space Agency's BepiColombo Mission Control Team at the European Space Operations Centre (ESOC) received the signal they had been waiting for – BepiColombo’s Mercury Transfer Module (MTM) successfully separated from the spacecraft stack. This landmark achievement for the ESA and Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) mission marks the first step of BepiColombo's long-awaited arrival at Mercury.
articles.summary: The European-Japanese BepiColombo mission successfully completes its Mercury Transfer Module separation, a critical milestone in approaching the smallest planet.

articles.title: Hubble tracks new decagon encircling Saturn’s south pole
articles.description: Recent observations with the NASA/ESA Hubble Space Telescope have revealed a giant, evolving 10-sided atmospheric wave encircling Saturn’s south pole. This discovery marks the first time a large regular-sided jet pattern has been observed in the planet’s southern hemisphere. The feature appears remarkably similar to Saturn’s famous hexagon at its northern pole, but is also distinctly different, suggesting scientists may be witnessing a new atmospheric phenomenon develop on the iconic gas giant.
articles.summary: Hubble observations reveal a newly evolving 10-sided atmospheric wave encircling Saturn's south pole, providing insights into the gas giant's dynamic atmosphere.

articles.title: Could the Clues to Ancient Alien Civilizations Be Hiding in a Bucket of Moon Dust?
articles.description: Most of our experience with the Search for Extraterrestrial Intelligence (SETI) has been focused on capturing radio signals that alien species have sent out, whether intentionally or unintentionally. That creates a huge “synchronicity” problem - what if there aren’t any alien civilizations broadcasting radio signals now, but there were a billion years ago? The Milky Way is around 13 billion years old - hoping that we exist at the same time as an alien civilization that happens to be actively messaging is a huge leap of faith. But, according to a new paper available in pre-print on arXiv and submitted to the International Journal of Astrobiology by Lewis J Pinault, as associated researcher at the SETI Institute, and his co-authors, we could take a completely alternative approach to trying to find alien civilizations - by looking for evidence of them in lunar dirt.
articles.summary: Researchers explore whether evidence of ancient extraterrestrial civilizations could be discovered within lunar samples through SETI methodologies.

articles.title: Dense Galaxies Are Carving Out A Bubble in the Early Universe
articles.description: Light could only travel freely in the Universe after cosmic reionization. Before that, neutral hydrogen stopped photons from travelling. The JWST has found evidence of an overdensity of galaxies carving out a bubble of reionization. Is this how it all started?
articles.summary: Dense galaxies in the early universe are carving out bubbles of ionized space, illuminating the epoch of cosmic reionization.

articles.title: How Big Can The Universe's First Starbursts Get?
articles.description: As our telescopes have improved and we’ve been able to peer farther back in time, we’ve begun finding more fascinating features of the universe. But one thing we definitely haven’t found yet is Population III (Pop III) stars. These were the earliest stars in the universe, formed completely from pristine hydrogen and helium, with no “metals” (i.e. elements heavier than those two) polluting their processes. They are also theorized to be absolutely massive, and “die with passion” as Bill Wurtz once put it in a famous YouTube video. A new paper, available in pre-print form on arXiv by Tae Bong Jeon from the Cosmic Frontier Center at the University of Texas at Austin, looks at just how massive those starbursts could be, and whether the James Webb Space Telescope could detect one.
articles.summary: Advanced telescopes reveal increasingly massive starburst galaxies in the early universe, challenging our understanding of initial star formation.

articles.title: What's Carving Active Gullies on Mars? It's Not Water
articles.description: Scientists were shocked when they received the first images of Martian gullies. They were even more shocked as those gullies appeared to change over time. Their similarities to gullies seen on Earth were uncanny, but all of Earth’s gullies are formed by the water run-off, and Martian is too cold and has too sparse an atmosphere to have liquid water on its surface. Whatever has been causing those changing gullies couldn’t have been water, so what was it? A new paper from Apolline Leclef of the Institut d’Astrophysique Spatiale at Université Paris-Saclay and her colleagues, available in pre-print on arXiv, shows how they are likely caused by CO2 frost turning into a fluid.
articles.summary: Scientists discover that active gullies on Mars are carved by processes other than water, revealing new insights into Martian geology.

articles.title: Japan's Hayabusa2 achieves first-ever laser ranging experiment with an asteroid
articles.description: The Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency's (JAXA) Hayabusa2 spacecraft reached another milestone this summer, a first for space agencies. On Sunday, July 5, the probe conducted the first successful laser-ranging experiment during a flyby of asteroid Torifune, the first exploration target of Hayabusa2's Extended Mission. This latest milestone will advance the capabilities of JAXA and other space agencies as they pursue future missions involving near-Earth asteroids (NEAs) and other deep-space objects.
articles.source: Space News - Space, Astronomy, Space Exploration
articles.summary: Japan's Hayabusa2 spacecraft successfully completes the first-ever laser ranging experiment on an asteroid, demonstrating advanced space technology.

articles.title: Rubin observatory peers deep into the famous COSMOS field
articles.description: The COSMOS field, or Cosmic Evolution Survey Deep Field, is one of the most famous patches of the universe observed by astronomers. Located in the constellation Sextans, this region was photographed by the Hubble Space Telescope (HST) in segments from 2003 to 2005 using its Advanced Camera for Surveys (ACS). With support from ground-based and other space-based telescopes, the resulting images were then stitched together to create a stunning picture of cosmic evolution.
articles.source: Space News - Space, Astronomy, Space Exploration
articles.summary: The Rubin observatory observes the renowned COSMOS field, one of the most extensively studied regions of the universe, yielding new cosmic insights.

articles.title: Scientists discover a strange new form of ice that could help explain the interiors of Neptune and Uranus
articles.description: Scientists have discovered that there is ice deep inside planets like Neptune and Uranus and want to find out what form it takes and how it behaves. They cannot dig for it and transport it all the way back to Earth, so they do the next best thing: recreate those extreme conditions in the lab.
articles.source: Space News - Space, Astronomy, Space Exploration
articles.summary: Scientists have discovered a new form of ice within Neptune and Uranus that offers crucial insights into these ice giants' planetary interiors. This finding advances our understanding of how these distant worlds formed and evolved.

articles.title: Physicists just found a tiny glitch in time itself
articles.description: Unconventional quantum theories may imply that time itself has a tiny fundamental uncertainty, placing an ultimate limit on how precisely any clock could measure it. The effect is far beyond current detection, but it could reveal a hidden connection between quantum mechanics, gravity, and spacetime.
articles.summary: Quantum physics research suggests time itself may have a fundamental uncertainty at the smallest scales, opening new frontiers in our understanding of reality. This discovery bridges quantum mechanics and fundamental physics in exciting ways.

articles.title: The Moon may have formed intact just hours after a giant collision
articles.description: Scientists have discovered that the Moon-forming collision may have depended heavily on how hot and physically strong early Earth and Theia were. New simulations found that some impacts create the familiar disk of debris that later becomes the Moon, while others can produce an intact Moon in only about five hours. The results challenge the long-standing assumption that the enormous collision could be modeled as if both worlds behaved mostly like fluids.
articles.summary: New research suggests the Moon may have formed intact within hours of a giant collision with Earth, revealing surprising insights into lunar formation. This discovery challenges previous assumptions about how quickly our Moon came into being.

articles.title: James Webb Space Telescope discovers the rings of tiny solar system body Chariklo are changing
articles.description: Using the James Webb Space Telescope, astronomers have discovered that the ring system of the tiny solar system body is even more interesting than they knew.
articles.summary: The James Webb Space Telescope has detected dynamic changes in the ring system of the tiny solar system body Chariklo. This breakthrough demonstrates the telescope's remarkable ability to observe subtle changes in distant solar system objects.

articles.title: Perseid meteors meet mesmerizing star trails over Egypt's Western Desert

articles.summary: Photographer captures stunning view of Perseid meteor shower cutting through star trails over Egypt's Western Desert, showcasing natural celestial phenomena.

articles.summary: NASA's Swift gamma-ray burst observatory ends its mission, celebrating its groundbreaking contributions to detecting cosmic explosions and high-energy astrophysics.

articles.description: Did icy comets deliver water to the young Earth? That idea won't go away. Now, astronomers at Lund University in Sweden have found evidence of exocomets orbiting a young star named PDS 70. The observations suggest that these comets are delivering water to tha…
articles.summary: Astronomers at Lund University discover icy exocomets around a distant star, providing new evidence for the theory that comets delivered water to early Earth.

articles.summary: NASA's Hubble detects a massive 10-sided atmospheric wave evolving around Saturn's south pole, offering rare insight into exotic planetary atmospheric phenomena.
